title: Lazy tokenizer prefetch + cost-aware SLA for runtime boundary
content:
Overview:
This note outlines a lightweight, pragmatic approach to push tokenization beyond the strict request boundary while keeping per-request latency predictable and cost-aware. The core idea is to adopt a lazy, prioritized prefetching layer for tokenization work and a token-span allocator that avoids full re-tokenization for small input edits. The design targets hosted + dedicated deployments; integrations with Private will be considered separately where disk/IO constraints differ.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Tokenization can be a measurable fraction of short-request latency (50–300ms depending on model/context).
- Re-tokenizing long shared prefixes (System / user history) across many concurrent requests wastes CPU and increases tail latency.
- Eager pre-tokenize-all is costly; doing nothing leads to repeated work and inconsistent latencies.
- We need a model that cooperates with batching, KV cache (prefix KV), backpressure, and cost/accounting (tokens billed).

Goals:
1) Reduce tokenization CPU for hot prefixes and repetitive traffic patterns without increasing 95/99 latency beyond configured SLA buckets.
2) Support batched tokenizers and per-request lazy paths with fallback to synchronous tokenization on miss.
3) Maintain accurate accounting (we must not double-bill or leak customer-visible token counts).
4) Keep system complexity bounded and incremental: instrumentation and rollout gates in console/optimize.

Non-goals:
- Global tokenizer refactor or replacing tokenizer implementation. This doc assumes current tokenizers (HF/BPE/unified) but adds orchestration.
- Deep language-specific normalization; we assume tokenizers are deterministic and idempotent.

High-level design:
1) Token-span allocator: a small service (in-memory lightweight per-runtime shard) that maps input text spans -> tokenized id arrays for hot prefixes. Allocator stores metadata: span hash, char range, token ids, token length, token offsets, and last-used timestamp. It is not a long-term KV store — eviction is LRU with TTL tuned per-deployment.

2) Lazy prefetch queue: when a request arrives, we compute cheap heuristics synchronously to identify likely reusable spans (e.g., conversation history prefixes, system prompts, instruction templates). If spans are hot and present in allocator, we reuse. If not present but judged high-probability (based on traffic statistics), we enqueue an asynchronous prefetch task for the span. Prefetch runs on pooled CPU workers and writes back to allocator on success.

3) Fast-path vs slow-path tokenization:
   - Fast-path: all required spans present in allocator -> stitch token arrays and return immediately.
   - Mixed-path: some spans present, others enqueued for prefetch -> the request can proceed after joining prefetch for critical spans only (see SLA rules) or proceed with on-the-fly tokenization for non-critical spans depending on policy.
   - Slow-path: no spans present and request cannot wait -> synchronous tokenization on requester thread.

4) Prefetch prioritization & cost-awareness: prefetch queue uses a priority that combines: observed reuse frequency, request latency budget, and estimated CPU cost (chars -> tokens). We attach a configurable cost multiplier so prefetching expensive long spans is deprioritized when system CPU is saturated or when tenant is in low-cost tier.

SLA policy integration (cost-aware SLA):
- Each request has an associated latency SLO bucket (e.g., interactive-50ms, interactive-200ms, background-500ms). The router populates a tokenization budget derived from SLO and current batching/queueing state.
- Prefetch can be speculative only if budget allows; otherwise, we fall back to synchronous tokenization on the critical path.
- For dedicated deployments, SLA config can allow more aggressive prefetch (larger background worker pool) since CPU is reserved. Hosted customers have per-tenant cost tags that can throttle prefetch to reduce chargeable CPU.

Interaction with KV prefix cache (runtime KV cache):
- We need to distinguish between tokenization allocator and model KV cache (decoder KV cache). They are complementary: allocator caches tokenized input spans (ids), KV cache caches past hidden states.
- Prefetch semantics: on allocation hit, we may avoid re-tokenization and also enable immediate KV cache lookup if a matching prefix ID is present in the KV cache store. To do so we store a small fingerprint in allocator entries (model id + tokenizer version + span hash) to ensure compatibility before reusing tokens into KV.
- Consistency rule: token ids are only reused if tokenizer version and normalization flags match exactly. If incompatible, we must re-tokenize. This prevents subtle off-by-one tokenization drift from producing invalid KV lookups.

Batched tokenizer execution:
- Batched CPU tokenization is beneficial for throughput but increases per-request latency variance. We propose two batched modes:
  1) Cooperative batching: short waiting window (e.g., 2–4ms) where request threads join a batch; batch size limited by latency bucket. This minimizes overhead but keeps tail low.
  2) Background batch worker: collects many spans for large background prefetch jobs (no tight latency bound).
- Requests on low-latency buckets should prefer cooperative batching or fast-path reuse; background batchers run only when request budget allows.
- Implementation detail: batch signature = tokenizer version + requested span type + normalization flags. Batching across heterogeneous spans is disallowed.

Backpressure and failure modes:
- If CPU worker pool is saturated, prefetch is throttled and priority demoted.
- On prefetch failure (timeout, exception), the runtime falls back to synchronous tokenization for that span. Errors are tagged for metrics; repeated failures for same span cause greylisting for a short period.
- Token-span allocator must guard against memory blowup: per-shard capacity + per-tenant cap. Eviction policy: LRU with rank bias for long-lived system prompts.

Accounting and billing implications:
- Tokenization performed by prefetch workers is chargeable CPU time; we must attribute prefetch CPU to a tenant when the span is tenant-specific (e.g., user conversation). For shared public system prompts or redwood-owned templates, charges are assigned to internal buckets.
- We must ensure token counts reported to customers reflect final tokens sent to the model; prefetching should not double-count tokens. Billing events only record tokens when the model request is executed, not when tokens are produced by prefetch.
- Add a debug flag to surface tokenization CPU per-request in logs for a short trial rollout.

Microbench plan (experiments):
1) Baseline: synchronous per-request tokenization with no allocator (existing prod binary). Measure p50/p95/p99 for short (<=64 char), medium (65–512 char) and long (>512 char) requests, CPU cycles, and cost per 1k requests.
2) Allocator cold-start: enable allocator but without prefetch (only populate on synchronous tokenization) to measure hit rate behavior.
3) Prefetch enabled: enable asynchronous prefetch with small worker pool (2 workers per shard) and cooperative batching. Tune heuristics threshold to hit ~40–60% hit rate for 1-week traffic trace.
4) Stress test: simulate traffic spikes, saturation, and measure degraded latency and drop in hit rate.

Measurements to collect:
- Tokenization CPU (ms & cycles) per request
- Allocator hit/miss ratio by span type
- Prefetch success rate and latency to availability
- Latency deltas for p50/p95/p99 vs baseline
- Memory footprint of allocator per shard and per-tenant
- Error/gap events: mismatched tokenizer versions causing re-tokenization

Rollout plan:
- Canary: opt-in for internal tenants; enable debug logs and fine-grained metrics. 1 day canary.
- Beta: 25% traffic across hosted API with strict telemetry. 7 days.
- Gradual ramp to 100% with rollback triggers: p99 latency increase > 10% or CPU cost increase > 15% vs baseline without tokenization savings.

Monitoring & alerts:
- SLA guardrails: alert when allocator hit-rate drops below threshold for 1 hour or p99 tokenization latency increases.
- Cost alert: when prefetch CPU attribution increases server-side cost by configurable amount.
- Integrity alert: spike in tokenizer-version-mismatch events.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should allocator fingerprints be canonicalized across model families? (helps reuse between similar LLMs with identical tokenizer versions).
- How to handle tenant-shared conversational histories (cross-tenant privacy)? Decide between shared public cache vs tenant scoping.
- Do we implement an adaptive TTL per-span based on observed reuse curve? (likely yes, requires telemetry.)
- UX: expose prefetch throttle settings in console and per-tenant overrides.
- Implementation spike: prototype allocator + prefetch in Rust service vs integration into existing runtime C++ process. Tradeoffs: cross-process reduces perf but isolates memory; integrated reduces RPC overhead.

Appendix: quick implementation notes:
- Span hashing: use 64-bit xxhash of UTF-8 normalized substring + tokenizer version + flags.
- Entry compact storage: store token ids as uint16[] for most vocab sizes; allow uint32 when needed. Keep offsets for partial stitching.
- Prefetch worker: use tokio-style async tasks or threadpool; measure GC/alloc pressure when using high churn.

Summary:
This design balances latency predictability with opportunistic CPU savings by shifting some tokenization work off the critical path while retaining per-request control via SLA-aware budgets. The implementation should start as a conservative canary and expand heuristics as we gain telemetry.

Next steps:
- Priya to prototype per-shard allocator sketch (2 days) -> GH PR 412
- Diego to run baseline microbench using 1 week anonymized traffic (3 days)
- Ava to draft console UI flags and cost attribution model (1 week)
- Team sync: RFC review on 2024-11-22 10:30am PT

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally pragmatic. Focus review on: compatibility guarantees with KV cache, billing attribution correctness, and fail-open semantics.
